paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: Thermodynamics has four main laws, and the zeroth law is one of them. It says that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, then they are also in thermal equilibrium with one another. Thermal equilibrium means this: the two systems are joined by a wall that lets only heat through, and neither of them changes over time.

paragraphs.heading: Who set it out
paragraphs.text: Ralph H. Fowler set the law out in the 1930s, well after the first, second and third laws had become widely recognized. It gives temperature a definition of its own, one that does not lean on entropy, the quantity defined by the second law.

paragraphs.heading: Other ways to say it
paragraphs.text: The law has been phrased in other ways too. James Clerk Maxwell summed it up as all heat being of one kind. Another version says that all diathermal walls are equivalent.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting systems into groups
paragraphs.text: In mathematical terms, the law makes thermal equilibrium an equivalence relation, a relation that can stand for two systems sharing an equal value of some quantity. Picture every system that is settled in its own internal equilibrium. These can be split into groups so that each system belongs to exactly one group, is in thermal equilibrium with all the others in it, and with no member of any other group. So each system can carry a unique tag: matching tags mean thermal equilibrium, different tags mean not. Empirical temperature is used as just such a tag.

paragraphs.heading: Why thermometers work
paragraphs.text: A quantity that comes out the same for any two systems that can sit in thermal equilibrium together is a temperature scale. The zeroth law is what such scales need, and it is what justifies using real thermometers. An ideal thermometer is one that does not noticeably change the system it measures. If it gives the same reading on two systems, they are in thermal equilibrium; if the readings differ, connecting the systems thermally changes both of them. The law says nothing, though, about what the final reading will be.

paragraphs.heading: What it leaves out
paragraphs.text: The law alone does not say which system is hotter or colder, or that temperatures run continuously from one to another. Those properties of order and continuity come from the temperature scales built on top of it. The second law supplies an absolute, or thermodynamic, temperature scale, and the zeroth law justifies using it. Today the main international definition of temperature is not this thermodynamic one but rests on the kinetic energy of freely moving tiny particles such as molecules, linked to temperature by the Boltzmann constant k_B.

paragraphs.heading: An example with gases
paragraphs.text: Two ideal gases in joint equilibrium across an immovable diathermal wall share the value P₁V₁/N₁ = P₂V₂/N₂, where P is pressure, V is volume and N is the amount of gas. Surfaces on which PV/N stays constant are therefore surfaces of equal thermodynamic temperature. Labelling them gives PV/N = RT, where R is a constant.
